clue.text: He is met in every walk of life

definitions.text: He is met in every walk of life

parts.words: He is met in every walk of life
parts.note: a walker on foot is met on every walk, and the word also means dull or everyday, met in every ordinary walk of life

explanation.surface: Some figure crops up among people of all classes and callings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walk of life' looks like a social phrase about careers, but read literally it is a stroll on foot, where you meet someone travelling on foot.
explanation.definitionFit: A person going on foot rather than by vehicle is met on every walk; the adjective also means commonplace.

clue.text: A spree would spoil 'their looks

indicators.note: to spoil something is to mess it up, so the letters of 'A spree' are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A wild night out would ruin someone's good looks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Would spoil' tells you to rearrange A SPREE; 'their' just links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To peer is to look closely, so peers as a verb means looks.

clue.text: A bit of sacking

parts.note: reads as a scrap of coarse sack cloth, but means one instance of firing someone from a job

explanation.surface: A scrap of coarse hessian cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sacking' looks like the rough fabric; it is being sacked from a job, and one case of that is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sacked is being fired from employment, and one such firing is a formal discharge.

clue.text: Given by a master magician?

parts.note: a schoolmaster gives a lesson, and a magician casts spells, so a teacher who is a wizard would teach 'spelling' in the other sense

explanation.surface: Something presented by a great conjuror.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Master' is a schoolmaster, so what he gives is a lesson; a magician deals in spells, so his lesson is on spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A class teaching how words are written puns on the spells a sorcerer casts.

clue.text: A quick descent causing such ill-feeling

definitions.meaning: running down a hill is a fast way down
feeling ... is being tired and unwell

explanation.walkthrough: 'Causing' only joins the two senses: the run down a slope, and the run-down feeling of being off-colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A dash down a slope is a quick descent; being worn out and poorly is feeling under the weather.

clue.text: Takes for granted it includes the whole lot

definitions.text: Takes for granted it includes the whole lot

parts.words: Takes for granted it includes the whole lot
parts.note: describes presuming without proof, while the word itself contains SUM, a word for a total or whole lot

explanation.surface: Someone presumes everything is covered by the deal.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening words define; the rest observes that the word written out contains SUM, the whole lot, in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: To presume something true without proof is to take it as given.

clue.text: Money that brings amusement to many

parts.note: amusement means fun
D is the Roman numeral for 500, a large number, so 'many'

explanation.surface: Cash that gives a lot of people a good time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Many' giving D relies on the Roman numeral 500, a crossword convention for a large number.
explanation.definitionFit: A fund is a sum of capital set aside for a purpose.

clue.text: The story one keeps in one's head

definitions.text: The story one keeps in one's head

parts.words: The story one keeps in one's head
parts.note: the '... storey' is slang for the head or brain, spelt here 'story' as Americans spell a building's floor

explanation.surface: A tale someone holds in memory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Story' is a floor of a building, not a tale; the upper storey is idiom for the head, where the mind lives.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'upper storey' is an idiom for the brain, the top floor of the body.

clue.text: Capital in divine surroundings with a railway to hump your luggage

indicators.note: the capital sits inside the abbreviation for a divine, which forms its surroundings

parts.note: DD, Doctor of Divinity, is a divine, here placed around
Rome is the capital of Italy

explanation.surface: A trip to a capital in pious company, using rail, with a beast to carry your bags.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts ROME inside DD (Doctor of Divinity, a divine). 'Hump' is a pun: the one-humped camel humps loads.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-humped camel is a pack animal, used to carry baggage across deserts.

clue.text: American-style batter

parts.note: reads like a pancake or fritter mix made the American way, but means a hitter in the American national game

explanation.surface: A pancake mix made the way they do it in the States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batter' looks like the cooking mixture; it is the one who bats, and the American way of batting is in that bat-and-ball sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone batting in America's national summer sport, rather than at cricket.

clue.text: Light entrance not only by these windows of Clough's

definitions.text: Light entrance not only by these windows of Clough's

parts.words: Light entrance not only by these windows of Clough's
parts.note: alludes to Arthur Hugh Clough's poem 'Say not the struggle nought availeth', whose lines say daylight comes in not only by the windows facing sunrise

explanation.surface: A line about sunlight getting in through a poet's windows.
explanation.walkthrough: Clough was a Victorian poet; his poem ends 'And not by ... windows only, / When daylight comes, comes in the light', the westward land is bright too.
explanation.definitionFit: Windows facing the sunrise, towards the orient, are those named in Clough's line.

clue.text: Operation that is often preset

parts.note: 'preset' reads as programmed in advance, but means done before a set, as a hairdresser washes hair before setting it

explanation.surface: A procedure usually programmed ahead of time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Preset' looks like a technical term for configured beforehand; read as pre-set it is what a hairdresser does before a shampoo and set.
explanation.definitionFit: A hair wash is the step a salon does before setting hair in curlers.

clue.text: Housekeeper's pantry not yet fully occupied ?

definitions.meaning: a store room in a large house where preserves, liqueurs and tea things were kept
if there is ..., a place is not yet full

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is an old country-house room, originally where cordials were distilled; the second reads as the phrase 'still room'.
explanation.definitionFit: A big house's storeroom for preserves; and a space with space left over is not yet full.

clue.text: High-flyer's starting point for yesterday's header into the lake

indicators.note: the first letter goes inside the lake's name, put into it

parts.note: Erie is one of the North American Great Lakes

indicators.note: the header of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Where yesterday's diver launched themselves before plunging into the lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Header' means a dive as well as the first letter: Y, the first of 'yesterday's', goes into ERIE. 'High-flyer' is an eagle, which starts from its nest.
explanation.definitionFit: An eagle's nest on a crag is where a soaring bird of prey begins its flights.

clue.text: Graduates at home for a clean-up here?

parts.note: BAs are Bachelors of Arts, graduates
in means at home

explanation.surface: University leavers staying in to tidy up.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowl of water for washing is where you clean your hands and face.

clue.text: They make greater obscurities of married life, we hear

indicators.note: says the phrase is heard spoken, so its sound gives a word spelt differently

parts.note: bigger mists are greater obscurities, things that cloud what is seen

explanation.surface: Some people make married life ever murkier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of married life' points at the answer: those with two spouses at once cloud wedded life. 'Greater obscurities' are BIGGER MISTS, which said aloud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: People who marry while already married are the subject of the clue's 'they'.

clue.text: A lasting distress includes love of one's old home

indicators.note: the anagram takes in the letter for love, which goes inside it
distress means damage or trouble, so the letters of 'A lasting' are thrown into disorder

parts.note: O is love, a score of zero in tennis

explanation.surface: A long-lasting sadness that holds a fondness for the house one grew up in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Distress' rearranges A LASTING; 'includes' then puts O (love, zero in tennis) inside. The definition is a longing 'of one's old home', the pining for home.
explanation.definitionFit: A wistful longing for the past or home is homesickness, originally the meaning of the Greek-made word.

clue.text: What you may be doing, oddly enough, in a lift

definitions.text: What you may be doing, oddly enough, in a lift

parts.words: What you may be doing, oddly enough, in a lift
parts.note: a lift suggests rising, so it is odd that riding it you may be travelling the other way, descending

explanation.surface: A remark about what happens to you in an elevator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lift' sounds like raising, which makes descending in one the 'odd' thing; a lift is British for an elevator.
explanation.definitionFit: Riding an elevator to a lower floor is descending, the opposite of what 'lift' suggests.

clue.text: Where clubmen meet

parts.note: clubmen reads as members of a gentlemen's club, but means players carrying clubs on a course

explanation.surface: The haunt of members of a gentlemen's club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubmen' looks like members of a London club; it means golfers, who carry clubs, and links is a seaside golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: A seaside golf course is where players with clubs gather.

clue.text: A midnight arrival, laden with honours

definitions.text: A midnight arrival, laden with honours

parts.words: A midnight arrival, laden with honours
parts.note: the turn of the calendar arrives at midnight on 31 December, and in Britain it brings the honours list

explanation.surface: Someone turning up at twelve, festooned with medals.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the monarch's New Year Honours list of knighthoods and medals is published on 1 January.
explanation.definitionFit: The start of January arrives at midnight and brings the British honours list.

clue.text: Artistic form of dottiness

parts.note: dottiness reads as eccentricity, but means painting or drawing in many small dots

explanation.surface: Creative eccentricity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dottiness' looks like madness; it is literally making dots, the artist's technique of shading with them.
explanation.definitionFit: Shading with many tiny dots of paint or ink is an artistic technique.

clue.text: No professionals from Italy

indicators.note: the letters are made from those of Italy, rearranged out of them

explanation.surface: There are no experts coming out of Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' asks for the answer to be made out of the letters of ITALY.
explanation.definitionFit: Lay people are those outside a profession or the clergy, so no professionals.

clue.text: Golden handshakes all round from him ?

definitions.text: Golden handshakes all round from him

parts.words: Golden handshakes all round from him
parts.note: a golden handshake is a large payoff, but this king turned everything he touched to gold, so his handshakes literally made gold

explanation.surface: A boss handing out generous severance packages to everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth King Midas turned whatever he touched to gold, so every handshake of his would be golden.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary Phrygian king whose touch turned all things to gold.

clue.text: You attain this by 16

parts.note: 16 down is descending, and by descending you reach a deep place, so how far down you have gone

explanation.surface: Something reached by the age of sixteen.
explanation.walkthrough: '16' looks like an age; it refers to 16 down, GOING DOWN, and going down gets you to a lower level.
explanation.definitionFit: How far down something reaches is what you gain by descending.

clue.text: A toy revolver

definitions.meaning: a spinning top or similar plaything
something that whirls round and round, not a pistol

explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolver' looks like a gun; it means anything that revolves.
explanation.definitionFit: A spinning plaything; and anything that whirls round is a thing that revolves.

clue.text: The patron saint of farmers ?

parts.note: Farmer ... is the stock English name for a farmer, so a saint of that name would suit them

explanation.surface: A question about which holy figure looks after agriculture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Farmer Giles' is a traditional British nickname for any farmer; St Giles is a real saint, though patron of cripples, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: St Giles shares his name with the proverbial English farmer.

clue.text: Sit after a little drink-? Just imagine!

indicators.note: the word for sit comes after the little drink in the answer

parts.note: to sup is to take a little drink, and a sup is a mouthful
to sit for a portrait is to pose

explanation.surface: Sit down after a sip of something, and just picture it!
explanation.definitionFit: To imagine a situation is to suppose it, picturing it as a hypothesis.

clue.text: Wages with bread for those on it?

definitions.text: Wages with bread for those on it?

parts.note: pay means wages
a roll is a small loaf of bread

explanation.surface: Earnings and a loaf for everybody listed.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: being on the list means receiving wages, and 'bread' is also slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: The list of employees and what they earn is what those on it are paid from.

clue.text: Part of London wherein to make a sporting call.

definitions.meaning: the district of the West End known for restaurants and nightlife
'...' was a huntsman's cry on sighting a hare

explanation.walkthrough: The London district is said to take its name from the old hunting cry; 'wherein to' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A West End district of London; and an old hunting halloo when a hare is seen.

clue.text: They're all down-to earth in the forest

definitions.text: They're all down-to earth in the forest

parts.words: They're all down-to earth in the forest
parts.note: down-to-earth reads as practical and sensible, but literally means reaching down into the soil, as the stems of woodland growth do

explanation.surface: A remark that everyone in the woods is sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down-to-earth' looks like a character trait; the main stems of woodland plants literally go down into the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: The main stems of woodland growth stand rooted in the ground.
